speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ACCEPTANCE BY PRIME MINISTER OF INVITATION BY PRESIDENT NIXON TO VISIT UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform the house I have accepted an invitation extended to me by President Nixon to pay an official visit to the United States. The President very thoughtfully suggested I come to Washington shortly following the conclusion of his tour of Europe to permit him to share with me his impressions of the current situation there. I am happy to say that arrangements convenient to both of us have now been completed. I shall travel to Washington for two days of talks on March 24 and 25. I look forward to this opportunity to meet the President personally and to discuss with him a wide range of questions which are of mutual concern to our two countries.
A more detailed program will be released later, once it has been worked out.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: ACCEPTANCE BY PRIME MINISTER OF INVITATION BY PRESIDENT NIXON TO VISIT UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am delighted, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister has received this invitation and is responding to it. I am sure this will provide an opportunity to improve relations between our country and the United States, which are so important to both countries.
We sometimes feel the weight of our great neighbour. I think we all agree there is very little that is more important to us in Canada than maintaining cordial relations between our country and the United States, together supporting our common interests and values in the world. The visit of the Prime Minister to Washington will provide a good opportunity to deepen the understanding between our two countries and their leaders.

subsubtopic: ACCEPTANCE BY PRIME MINISTER OF INVITATION BY PRESIDENT NIXON TO VISIT UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that members in all parts of the house will be pleased the Prime Minister has received this invitation and that he proposes to accept it.
At this stage in world development I think it is increasingly important that the leaders of these two countries should discuss the many problems we have in common. I hope the Prime Minister will avail himself of this opportunity to impress upon the United States that while Canada wants to co-operate with our neighbour, at the same time there are measures which Canada must contemplate in order to strengthen our independence as a sovereign nation. That covers a great many items of which I am sure the Prime Minister is fully aware. We all wish him well in these discussions, and hope he will be able to give a favourable report when he returns.

I do not like the way tfiose bills have been brought before the house. Although I do not question the government's good intentions in introducing amendments to agricultural legislation, I have grave doubts about the legality of certain procedures set out in those amendments. Those engaged in agriculture will have to avail themselves of a cumbersome machinery if they are to take advantage of the provisions of recent amendments.
When Bill C-156 first came before the house the members of my party protested the provision in it that would enable a government appointed inspector to seize animals or produce. We also protested the fact that appeals could only be brought to the assessor appointed by the government. A similar provision has been incorporated in other bills recently before this house. Furthermore the decision of the government appointed assessor is final, there can be no appeal to any court. It seems that the government has done all it

I point out to the bouse that the wording of section 14A(3), on page 2 of the bill, is in part as follows:
The provisions of Part II of the Pesticide Residue Compensation Act, with such modifications as circumstances require,-
The meaning of those words is clear. Once this bill has been passed by parliament, regulations to be drafted can only have the effect of curtailing the rights of farmers. At this point we have no idea what those "modifications as circumstances require" will be. I think the government is going about its business in the wrong way. We are giving a blank cheque to departmental officials when we tell them they may draw such regulations as circumstances may require. That language in the bill is absolutely unfair to the agricultural industry. In essence, those words mean that those drafting the regulations are responsible to one party only in any dispute, the government. Naturally they are duty-bound by their very occupation, sense of responsibility and obligation to ensure in each instance that the actions, intent and welfare of the government department are well protected. As I said previously, the original intent of the bill may have been good but the regulations are all one-sided. It is almost impossible for individual farmers or co-operatives in many instances to seek the redress which is available to other citizens and industries in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this bill was studied in committee and is now at the final stage of discussion in the house. The bill sets out the level of compensation to which a farmer or producer is entitled. As was stated by the previous speaker, the amount of compensation will be set by the Governor in Council or the government in their wisdom. On appeal the farmer or producer is limited to the compensation set by the Governor in Council.
The bill provides that there may be an appeal to an assessor where no maximum amount of compensation has been prescribed for an animal pursuant to section 12, or where the compensation awarded to the farmer is less than the maximum compensation prescribed under the act, or where no compensation is awarded to the farmer, on the ground that the failure to award compensation was unreasonable. It is within these limits that any individual who feels he has been unjustly dealt with must appeal. As I understand the bill, a farmer or producer cannot go to a court and claim that the basic amount of compensation set by the Governor in Council is wrong.
I give the government credit for their attempt to move forward in this field in order to deal more effectively and fairly with the farmer and producer. However, the fact is they have reserved for themselves the right to decide when they are being fair and when they are not. This is tfie point at issue. It is for this reason I feel they are more concerned about protecting the government than protecting the position of the farmer.

Mr. Speaker, I should like once again to draw the minister's attention to the matter of compensation to be paid for pure-bred and grade animals.
I suggest that this question has not been thoroughly looked into by the committee. I do not know whether they are trying to ignore the situation or will not face up to the facte, but I wish to tell the minister that a review of the situation prevailing not only in our area but all over Canada would reveal that 60 to 75 per cent of our dairy cattle are grade animals.
And this is not a whim of the people but just an effort to get a better yield.

I know a number of farmers who have marvelous Holstein herds, for instance, mixed with Ayrshire or Canadian breeds. In our cold areas, where it is difficult to get a top quality herd, I know of-and I have no hesitation at all in saying so-a number of grade dairy herds which are superior to some purebred herds.
In my opinion, when you think that a farmer will receive for his grade animals a compensation equal to 50 per cent of their normal value, when at the productive and commercial level his animals are worth as much as pure-bred animals, I have no hesitation in saying that he is discriminated against.
I have already called the attention of the minister to this point and I think that the officials will have to take the trouble to consider the situation which prevails in our areas-I am referring mainly to my own-in order to assess the degree of injustice suffered in the past.
Last year mention was made of dairy producers who had incurred tremendous losses. One of them for instance had lost 95 good dairy cows and he managed to recover only 50 per cent of their value because his animals were not pure-bred. However, they had been selected for the past 25 years which means that this farmer, like a number of others, incurred a tremendous loss. I have mentioned only one case in passing but 80 per cent of the herds in my area have been affected by contagious diseases and the farmers have paid dearly for the simple fact that they own grade animals.
Therefore, I ask the minister as well as the specialists-since there are some and since they are capable of judging such cases-to study this problem which is most important for our agriculture, in view of the high percentage of grade herds that we find in our areas.
I think that the case of a farmer who devoted 20 or 25 years to build up a good herd and who gets from the government, in case of an outbreak of contagious disease, a compensation that is 50 per cent of what others get, represents, I think, an example of the grave injustice that is sometimes inflicted on the farmers of our area.
I think it would be preferable, from now on, to take as a base the value of the dairy production of the herd in order to compensate the farmer and to treat him more fairly instead of considering the colour, the weight or the breed of the animal.

The old law provided a certain amount for pure-bred animals as well as for grade animals. The department now works according to regulations. The legislation is passed, the general principle of the bill is approved and then we have to wait for the regulations that are to be enacted by the department's officials. That is not really democratic, I believe, because the representatives of the people have absolutely no say in the drafting of those regulations. I should like us to be able, as in previous years, to know where we stand. We should no longer have to wait for a lav/ to be passed in the hope that the enacted regulations will be in accordance with it.
I once experienced difficulties with such a system of regulations, perhaps not with regard to agriculture but housing, for instance. I have already mentioned this in the house when I indicated that the regulations went against the legislation we had passed.
However, there is a danger, that of two or three less able officials who might turn up some day and change the regulations because they are allowed to do so every year or every six months, at will. The enforcement of this law, which is basically good, might be hampered by regulations which would not be adapted to it.

As for the right to appeal, I think that the three months' period is quite a reasonable one. However sometimes it is not enough because of all the red tape involved and mainly because the farmers lack information.
I would want the officials in charge of enforcing this law to go on dealing with complaints, just as they used to do, once the deadline has been reached. More often than not, whether through ignorance or otherwise, the farmer has proved unable to meet such deadline. Farmers are not here in the house to follow our proceedings and they need some time to learn all about the law. Indeed, at such times when, as it has happened for the past few years, there is an outbreak of contagious disease, they are apt to panic and to lose their heads. And when they have finally picked themselves up and want to direct their requests through the proper channels, the three months' period mentioned in the law is over.
I shall deal very briefly with the third point. I have had many complaints with regard to the disposal of the carcasses of sick animals which problem has caused me many difficulties. It is understood that the farmer gets compensation for the animal, but he must sell the meat.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the fact that the farmer has to sell a dead animal to a recognized slaughter house lends itself to criticism. Of course, criticism must be avoided as much as possible, but it is rather difficult. I think much of the criticism is due to the fact that often the farmers feel that some slaughter houses take advantage of the situation to pay a ridiculously low price for the meat while, most of the time, the meat is worth as much as if the animal had not been killed because of disease.
This is another question that should be studied by the minister and his staff. I do not wanted to dwell on the matter unduly, because it is rather touchy; we are dealing with buyers and sellers, which means that this is really a family quarrel. I merely wish to point out to those who will apply these bills in the future, that when they get a complaint they should weigh the pros and cons in order to do justice, not only to the slaughter house but to the interested parties in the first instance, the farmers, who in addition to having lost cattle because of an epidemic must also lose 50 per cent on the value of the meat when the cattle is taken to the slaughter house.

Mr. Speaker, those were the remarks I wanted to draw to the intention of the minister and his staff. I trust they will help to-correct some of the deficiencies that have existed in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that this bill is designed only to modernize the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. This it does to some extent. The compensation formerly paid under this act was $140-each for purebreds and $70 each for grade cattle slaughtered under any herd disease eradication program. It must be admitted that these figures are ridiculously low at the present time. The bill proposes to change them to amounts to be prescribed by the Governor in Council. It is my understanding that the proposed amounts are $120 for grade animals and $200 for purebreds. These figures are more realistic especially when applied to beef cattle where the salvage value of the carcass may be higher. However, this is certainly open to argument, and I am sure that the beef producers might argue the point.
In the case of dairy cattle these amounts may be much too low. I think it would be fairer to ensure to the owner a percentage of the replacement value of the animal. At the present stage in the improvement of dairy herds most so-called dairy cows are the result of artificial breeding for many generations. The value of these animals is therefore much higher than what the value of a grade animal used to be. There could be great discrimination in the case of a man who has a herd which becomes infected by a disease. Many animals of this type are very high producers, and the producer may have been raising them for many years.
The number of reactors to tests for bovine t.b. and brucellosis or contagious abortion is much less now than it has been in the past. This points to the success of the establishment of disease-free areas, testing for both diseases, and calfhood vaccination against brucellosis. Adequate compensation for the relatively few animals that must be condemned would not place much strain on the economy and would ensure the maximum cooperation of the herd owner.
I can understand the reason for slowing down the calfhood vaccination program at this point since it does interfere with later testing and causes problems in respect of

export In some cases the disinfecting of premises could be very costly and an additional hardship to the owner who has already suffered some hardship if he has had reactors. So I think some aid here would be in order.
I should like for a moment to refer to the clauses which deal with an appeal to the assessor. Mr. Speaker, my intervention in this debate is on the same basis as my intervention in respect of Bill C-155. I have been horrified by what I consider to be a massive bureaucratic assault on civil liberties involved in bills dealing with what are relatively minor problems although problems which merit consideration. We protest against the method being adopted. I recant nothing I said with regard to Bill C-155. Here again, as a result of some rather wrong drafting, by importing into one bill provisions of another bill that are not related, some of the objectionable features of Bill C-155 have been brought into Bill C-156. The minister was not present at some committee hearings where I said a great deal about what I think is a slipshod method of drafting. An individual who is interested in this act can obtain an office consolidation of the act, but he will find that it refers him to another act and back and forth he will have to go. I complained most bitterly about this procedure in respect of Bill S-4, an act dealing with the marking of articles made from precious metals. Suddenly, by reference, we found ourselves involved with the Fisheries Act because it dealt with the method of disposing of goods which had been seized. There is nothing worse than having to sort out this type of thing.
First of all, I have said this bill is bad from a drafting point of view. Second, I come back to the point about the non-requirement of publication of regulations. I and other members of the opposition will keep insisting that there must be a requirement within the act itself and not just a reliance upon the government. There must be a requirement that any

Animal Contagious Diseases Act regulation made under the act will be tabled in parliament.
We have gone to a good deal of trouble to set up a committee on statutory instruments. It is in its preparatory stages, but the intent is to review all delegated legislation. This can be done if the regulations are tabled. It is not sufficient merely to say that they may be published in the Canada Gazette. As the minister knows, having sat with me on the procedure committee, we may also acquire a cumulative index of documents tabled by the ministry so that members will know where they are.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I do not know why there is resistance and seeming reluctance to take what appear to be sensible steps to publicize the approved regulations. I recognize the fact that regulations must be made under most acts. Certainly you cannot spell out everything in statutory form. But what is wrong with requiring under the act that all regulations be published?
The minister may be the most benevolent despot there is; he may say that we can rest assured that as long as he is the minister every regulation under the jurisdiction of his department will be published. He may even go farther and seek leave of the house to table them. That may be the minister's own view but we must remember that he is exercising his own discretion. The minister is not immortal and this act is not just for a year or so. Ministers come and go. Sometimes they are promoted, sometimes they are demoted and sometimes they are defeated.
Sometimes they die.

Yes, and sometimes they are incapacitated.
Notwithstanding all the good wishes and the intentions of the minister, I will let him in on another secret. Anything the minister says and any undertaking he makes during the debate is not worth one farthing in a court of law. It is meaningless in binding him or his officials in a court of law. The assessors, who will presumably conduct themselves as judges, will say that nothing said in parliament is meaningful in so far as the interpretation of the regulations or the statute is concerned.
For this reason I should like it written into the act that any regulations shall be tabled within 15 days after the coming into force thereof or, if the house is not then sitting, within ten sitting days of the opening of the

Animal Contagious Diseases Act session. This is how we do things in respect of many bills. Why was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) so happy to do this in respect of the anti-dumping bill? There was no quarrelling about this on the part of the officials of the Department of Finance in respect of that measure or in respect of the Bank Act, for example. I do not see what is wrong with it.
Let me go one step further. Not only should the regulations made by the Governor in Council and the regulations made by the assessors be publicized but the rules ini respect of the conduct of hearings must be made known. I point out that in so far as the rules for the determination of assessments are concerned, these are to be made by the assessors subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. They are not regulations made by the Governor in Council. Therefore I put it to the minister that they would not be regulations required to be tabled or published under the Regulations Act. Why can they not be published?
They will be.

The minister may say what he wants, but they will not necessarily be published because there are no requirements for them to be published. We do not legislate on the basis of good intentions. The road to Hades is paved with good intentions.
I am not going there so I don't know.

Perhaps the minister and I will meet up there. But let me say this. Why can we not have in this legislation this simple provision in respect of the regulations? I will have the same thing to say about Bill C-157.
The next question I want to ask is, why is it that Supreme Court or Exchequer Court judges have been chosen to be assessors? The minister's colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), and his predecessor have fulminated against this practice in this house. I do not know how many times the bar association and law societies have complained about the use of judges in extra-judicial proceedings. This practice has caused grave complaint. Nothing is said in this bill in respect of their remuneration. Are they to be

remunerated on a per diem basis for taking on this non-judicial work? There is nothing in the measure which says anything about that. It is a serious cause for complaint that some judges have a predilection for taking on extra-judicial work because it gives them a greater return over and above their salaries.
Apparently judges are going to be named as assessors either under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act or the Pesticide Residue Compensation Act. I suggest it would be far better for the minister to appoint other people as assessors. It is possible to find men who are well qualified to act as assessors and then provide the right of appeal to a court. Let me tell the minister something more in respect of the powers of the assessor. He says he will appoint assessors. The assessor is the one who will actually hear the appeals. wrong. The proposed method of operation of the bill is wrong. Mr. Speaker, clause 1 of Bill C-156 repeals the provisions of paragraphs (a) and (b) of subjection 2 of section 12 of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act and sets out new provisions with regard

Animal Contagious Diseases Act to compensation for animals slaughtered under a disease eradication program. The bill gives to the Governor in Council the power to set rates of compensation which in the opinion of the government are deemed to be equitable. On the face of it this is little more than an empty gesture by the minister. Even though the assessor appointed may be a judge, in this situation he will be nothing more than a government employee. It seems to me this is a poor way for the government to arrive at an equitable decision as to the amount of compensation that should be paid. I join the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in protesting against the fact that there is no appeal from the decision of the assessor. We will put out a newsletter.

The house resumed at 2 p.m.

When the house rose at one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, we were dealing with Bill C-156, an act to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. More specifically, we were considering the matter of an increase in compensation to farmers or producers for animals slaughtered under an area or herd disease eradication program.
The bill has been reviewed at some length by the Standing Committee on Agriculture, and in the committee sessions a considerable debate took place on new section 14A which has to do with the right of appeal. Along with other members of the committee I took strong exception to the implications of this section. I do not intend to belabour the point because I believe several other members of our party, much more capable of dealing with it because of their legal training, will be speaking on this important aspect of the legislation. In fact, several of my hon. friends have already done so, including the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who dealt with it at some length before the lunch break,

Animal Contagious Diseases Act the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Dan-forth) and our house leader the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin).
I should like to question for a few moments certain aspects of clause 3 (1) of the bill which deals with the coming into force of this legislation and with making the payment of claims retroactive to September 26, 1968. How are these claims to be assessed? First of all, will each of these cases be reviewed automatically? Second, must a farmer make an application or an appeal on the basis of a former settlement? The bill stipulates that an applicant can make an appeal within three months. My third question is: in the light of the fact that it is now February 21, six months later than the date I mentioned, how is an appellant likely to be affected? Hon. members will note that no maximum or minimum amounts with respect to compensation are set out in the bill. Since some farmers may already have secured compensation under the terms of the old act, how are the officials, in appraising a claim under the new act, to determine the amount of compensation to be paid?
It seems to me that complications may well arise as a result of the failure to specify maximum and minimum amounts. I recall that in the committee we tried very hard to establish maxima and minima so that there might be at least an indication of the amount of compensation a farmer would receive. I believe difficulties are likely to arise in this connection. To put it in other words, farmers may be doubtful that it would be worth their while to appeal in the first place.
I could raise a number of other questions in connection with the bill but I know some of my hon. friends will be referring to them. Therefore I shall conclude my remarks by expressing the hope that the minister will explain the aspects of the legislation to which I have drawn attention.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you for giving me the opportunity of expressing my opinion on third reading of Bill C-156.
I am aware that some improvements are found in this legislation, nevertheless, I have a few reservations to make. I sincerely believe that it does not go far enough; more details could have been incorporated into the text of the bill. I know that the compensation rate which was fixed to make up for the losses of animals caused by contagious
February 21. 1969

Animal Contagious Diseases Act diseases was, in a way, limited to a certain amount by the former act.
If amendments were incorporated in the act, it is because it was necessary to do away with those figures, in order to determine new ones better adapted to the current market. However, the act provides that the governor in council may prescribe the maximum compensations. If in so doing, account is taken of the various factors that should effectively be considered to determine the actual value of an animal, we can expect improvements. In fact, if I understood well the explanations given by the minister to the standing committee on agriculture, those are maximums which will be reviewed from time to time so that they will always be in relation with the actual market value.
It would be advisable, however, that the Department of Agriculture could take the necessary arrangements to inform animal owners about the maximum rates prescribed for the various types of animals so that owners can determine a little in advance the amount which will be awarded to them to compensate eventual losses.
I know that previously this legislation was only applicable to the species mentioned in the law, i.e. horses and cattle, but I am wondering whether it would not be possible to include also sheep and hogs, because contagious diseases also strike those animals down and their owners often sustain damages which quite often are not reasonably compensated. At all events, I am suggesting this to the minister and I hope he will give consideration to it.
I seize this opportunity to draw to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) the fact that breeders and farmers also suffer considerable damage.
I have often received complaints from breeders who send their animals to the slaughter house and when the grading is done, they find that 10 per cent of their herd is condemned or downgraded, which causes them a considerable loss. The disease is determined by competent people who condemn these animals. In my opinion, these losses should be provided for under a law which would enable the breeders to receive a compensation, because profits in this field are not very high already.
As far as the right of appeal is concerned, I think this bill is an improvement. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has dealt with the judicial aspects of the matter a few minutes ago. I do not feel qualified

to discuss the judicial aspect of this bill; however, I shall deal with its practical aspect.
Under the former legislation, that right of appeal did not exist. Since it now exists, if it not complicated by red tape which makes an appeal impossible, I think that the owner of the seized cattle could launch an appeal and hope that as soon as possible and not in 5 or 10 years, justice will be rendered to him. Now, it is really an improvement.
The legislation is made by human beings; they cannot be perfect, even if the Department of Agriculture is well-intentioned and accepts suggestions liable to improve legislation parliament is called upon to pass in the agricultural field as well as in others.
I think that members of the committee on agriculture made serious suggestions to convince the minister to establish reliable rates to determine the value of an animal. Then, the minister got out of it so well with wise arguments that the bill was not amended.
At this third reading stage, I wonder if we could not take those amendments in consideration. Any way, as a whole, the bill eliminates an injustice against breeders of top grade animals, because the real value was not considered under all its aspects. If the officials of the Department of Agriculture responsible for the application of the law takes all appropriate measures to give justice to producers then we could say that the legislation is an improvement to be welcomed.
In any event, there will surely be other sessions, and the act, in its present wording, will probably be passed by the government. Next year, an opportunity may be offered to amend it and I rely on the minister's sense of responsibility and honesty to do so, taking into account the recommendations and the suggestions to which the deficiencies of the present act may have given rise.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-156, to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, has to do with the compensation which will be paid to farmers and livestock owners for animals condemned to be slaughtered because they have been infected with brucellosis, tuberculosis or other contagious diseases. This is a good amendment. It provides that from time to time the maximum amount of compensation to be paid shall be decreed by regulation instead of being fixed by statute. In other words, the act need not
February 21. 1969	COMMONS
be amended to provide for increased amounts of compensation.
Hon. members of the opposition have suggested this amendment is not too important since only a few thousand farmers or livestock operators will be affected each year. One cannot over-emphasize the importance to this country of the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. They are the cornerstone on which a healthy livestock industry in Canada may be built. Hon. members will recall that in 1951 there was an outbreak of foot and mouth disease in Canada, with economic repercussions that represented the loss of many millions of dollars. It is most important that the border between Canada and the United States should be open for the unrestricted export of our cattle.
We discussed these amendments in the Standing Committee on Agriculture. Although the suggestion was made that the maximum amount of compensation to be paid on grade animals should be $120 and on purebred animals $200, I hope the minister will reconsider these amounts since I feel the figures set out in the regulations should have some bearing on the actual loss suffered by a farmer. The suggested figures may be adequate to compensate for ordinary, grade cattle and other animals. For high yield dairy animals the figures are not adequate. I suggest the compensation figure ought to represent the difference between the price realized at slaughter and the actual, market value of a similar, healthy animal. Such a provision will not cost the government very much money. Of 4,000 head of cattle condemned to be slaughtered least year only 8 per cent were purebreds.
An hon. member of the opposition suggested that compensation should be equal to 80 per cent of the actual market value of the animal that has been condemned. I think the figure ought to be close to 100 per cent. After all, the farmer has the expense of disposing of the animal, no matter what its stage of lactation is. The value of the animal may vary according to time of year. In addition to losing the animal the farmer must also pay for the cost of disinfecting and cleaning his premises. For very good or very poor farmers, that constitutes no great problem. The farmer with a first-class diary operation has his buildings in excellent condition and has no problem in disinfecting them. Similarly, the farmer with buildings consisting of a shed with a straw roof and some huts can touch a match to his property and burn it down. No
DEBATES	5813
Animal Contagious Diseases Act great trouble or expense is involved there. The majority of farmers lie between these extremes. Sometimes they may not have whitewashed or disinfected their buildings for many years and the cost of so doing is considerable. The costs incurred in such operations ought to be considered in the bill.
It is good to find an appeal provision in the bill. This is a fundamental right we expect to see included in government regulations of this type. The appeal machinery will be used seldom. As I said, there are only 3,000 to 4,000 compensation claims per year. Usually they are handled amicably by the inspector and the livestock owner. The appeal machinery will be used only where disputes arise.
In conclusion I wish to say this is a good amendment which will bring the act up to date and enable maximum amounts of compensation to be set by regulation.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make two or three observations. Undoubtedly future amounts of compensation paid under the act will increase. The bill has provisions allowing for great flexibility in that maximum amounts of compensation may be set from time to time by regulations. A government appointed inspector will investigate compensation claims and act on behalf of the government in a manner prescribed by regulation. The possibility of an appeal by a farmer to an assessor has been incorporated in the bill. In the future there will be many more cases of compensation and more appeals as more and more chemicals are used. The need for compensation will arise in many different ways and under different circumstances.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Under this bill, the assessor is closely bound by the regulations. Mr. Jack McIntosh (Swift Current-Maple
Creek): Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) has left the house as I was going to compliment him on a very good speech. I agree with most of his remarks. However, I disagree with his closing comment with regard to the appeal clause, new section 14A. I suggest to him with all due respect that it makes a mockery of the word "appeal". It is not an appeal at all.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) asked the minister why this clause was even being included in the act. The minister's reply was that it was not there before. This will become the law. Under British justice any individual in Canada can appeal to the courts on points of law. This right has been taken away from those who raise cattle. They must now appeal to an assessor, the department or the minister. An appeal from what? From what the assessor, the department and the minister have said. This is no appeal. The right of an individual to appeal has been taken away by this clause. I agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West when he stated a few moments ago that this is very untidy administration and untidy housekeeping.
New section 14A (3) reads:
The provisions of Part II of the Pesticide Residue Compensation Act, with such modifications as circumstances require, apply to appeals brought under this Act.
In whose opinion and under what circumstances are these modifications necessary? Will they be prescribed by the assessor, the department and the minister? Does the appellant have no rights whatsoever? What justice is there in appealing to the minister from a statement by his assessor or his department? Is this the just society? A colonel I know used to say, "I believe in democracy, but this is the way I want it done and, by God, this is the way it is going to be done." That is what the minister has said. Appeal? This is a mockery of appeal.
The hon. member for Edmonton West coined a phrase which I think is appropriate.
[Mr Ritchie.]
He called this provision a bureaucratic assault. It must have been officials of the minister's department who advised him. Surely they have enough trouble already with accusations of bureaucratic dictatorship being hurled at them in this house, by our constituents, and in the press. These officials are building up a bureaucratic dictatorship by taking away the right of the individual to appeal to the courts of our land. When speaking the other night on Bill C-155 I stated that the people of Canada can do without this type of legislation. We are losing more rights every day in this just society. I appeal to the minister to leave it as it was. We are quite satisfied that we have the right to appeal to the courts under our present system.
Under British justice this is the right of every individual in Canada.. There are very few acts which do not allow the right of appeal to the courts. There is one section of the Income Tax Act which states that an individual is guilty until he proves his innocence. There is also one clause in the Canada Pension Plan which does not allow the right of appeal. This is contrary to our system of British justice. We as members of parliament have shirked our responsibility in this regard. This responsibility must be taken away from the bureaucrats and given back to the house. It is not the responsibility of these commissions which the government has set up. I do not think it is necessary to name them. They are doing a good job under our instructions. We are the ones at fault, not them. The Canada Pension Plan states that the interpretation of that act is the sole responsibility of the commission. That is not justice. Although it was done for a reason at the time, I think it should be changed.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
The minister stated that judges of our courts would be appointed assessors. This is another responsibility that judges should not have. As one of my colleagues said a few moments ago, this will take away from their dignity as judges in our courts. It makes them a political tool of the government of the day, and judges do not like to be met with an accusation of political patronage. Under this legislation I can see circumstances arising when from time to time there will be accusations of political patronage, and I am quite sure the senior judges will frown on those who accept this type of work. I do not know what compulsion the minister can use to make judges accept it, but I am sure if it were left to their own decision they would

not want to act in this capacity knowing it would place them in an impossible position. I again appeal to the minister to withdraw this clause because it will do more harm than good.

Mr. Speaker, we are being asked to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. We should avoid doing so at all times, and I want to be on record as opposing that part of the bill.
Since it is evident that the bill will be passed, I would like to know what protection members of parliament and the taxpayers of Canada generally will have following the granting of this ministerial discretion. How and where will we find a list of the names and addresses of those people who are paid compensation? Will it be published in the Canada Gazette? It used to appear in the estimates under "Compensation to Breeders" in the health of animals section. There used to be a list of names and addresses of those who had been paid compensation in cases where the circumstances were not covered by the act and the regulations, but that has disappeared. I could not find such a list in the public accounts for 1967.
I suggest to the minister that it would not be a bad idea if the names and addresses, and the amounts involved, were published monthly and sent to all the breeder organizations so that the public may see what is going on and that nothing is kept from the view of the public. There is one provision which appears in the estimates every year with the heading, "in circumstances not covered by the act". Some $8,000 was estimated under it last year. I have an idea that it covers animals that die in transit or in accidents before the amount of compensation is arrived at, but I would like the minister to confirm this. Against my better judgment I shall agree to giving this discretionary power to the minister or whomsoever he may appoint, but it is

Mr. Speaker, at first glance this legislation would appear to affect only a relatively small number of people, and the minister and the government may be disposed to feel that because only a relatively small number of persons may be affected they are at liberty to take very unusual steps in the legislation. I point out that even if only a small number of farmers are affected this house has a responsibility to protect the inalienable rights of every citizen, and that any injustice perpetrated against even one person is something this house must attempt to guard against.
However, this legislation, as I understand it could affect a very large number of persons. I recall that on the prairies a few years ago, when we had an epidemic of foot and mouth disease, hundreds of farmers were required to have their cattle slaughtered and the question of compensation was a very live, controversial and bitter one. As I look at this bill I cannot help wondering whether if it were dealing with mining companies, oil companies or other large corporations, legislation of this type would be introduced by the government, because this legislation deprives certain Canadian citizens under certain circumstances of some of their basic, inalienable rights.
I think the minister is wise in taking out of the act the stipulated figures with respect to the compensation which will be paid. With inflation continuing at the rate it is, I do not think you can put in a statute now the maximum amount that will be paid for either grade or purebred cattle that may have to be destroyed next year, two years from now or five years from now. Unless you are going to amend the act every year, any table of set compensation would very rapidly become obsolete. Therefore the minister has to ask the house, and I think in this case properly, for the authority to recommend to his colleagues in cabinet that an order in council be passed setting forth what the maximum compensation will be.
However, Mr. Speaker, it should be remembered that what is happening is that the government, which is going to pay the compensation, is the one which by regulation will determine the compensation. That, by the very nature of things, is quite dictatorial. It cannot be prevented, but that is the situation. The government, which itself must pay the
Animal Contagious Diseases Act compensation, is going to say by order in council what that compensation will be, or at least the maximum amount for which it will be liable.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Properly speaking there must be a right of appeal. The appeal is to be made to an assessor, but the assessor is not a free agent. Under the legislation before us he is confined within the maximum that the government has set. So the government, which must pay compensation, is stating by order in council what the maximum compensation shall be. Then it appoints an assessor who is to hear the appeal but tells him that the figure which has been set is sacrosanct and that he dare not go beyond it. He dare not go beyond the maximum. By what moral or legal judgment does the cabinet decide that the maximum which they set is an inviolate figure? If there is to be an appeal, surely that appeal ought to be to someone who is in a position to say that the figure which the cabinet has set at some previous time is no longer adequate and that in the opinion of the assessor the particular animal being slaughtered is worth more than the amount set by the government in the order in council. The assessor should have the right to recommend any figure which he thinks is in keeping with the situation.
It makes a farce of the whole question of appeal to say that a farmer will have the right of appeal and then in the next breath say that the assessor wjio is to hear the appeal will be limited to making his judgment within a maximum set by the very government which will have to pay the compensation. If ever there was a case of a government wanting to be the judge, jury and prosecuting attorney all in one, surely this is it. Then I believe the final indignity is to state that the decision of the assessor on any appeal brought pursuant to this part is final and conclusive and not subject to appeal to or review by any court.
I understand that my colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) attempted to amend Bill C-155 when that bill was before us. His amendment was with reference to a clause which is applicable now in this bill, C-156. I cannot condemn in too strong terms the fact that the government would ask the house to write into the statute books a specific prohibition against the right of appeal to the courts. Surely this ought to be a basic right. As a matter of fact, some of us have fought for years to have established

February 21, 1969
as a principle of law in this country that any individual can sue the Crown without a fiat from the Minister of Justice or the Attorney General of a province. During the time I had the privilege of being associated with a provincial government we removed the requirement that a fiat had to be secured in order to sue the Crown. If in our present society governments must acquire more and more power, which is the situation in a society as complex and complicated as ours, then surely the citizen should have as a last resort the right to sue the Crown when he or she feels an injustice has been done.
Hear, hear.

Instead of moving in that direction and removing the requirement that a fiat must be secured in order to sue the Crown, we are now asked to place on the statute books a specific prohibition against the right to sue the Crown. The government really is saying to a farmer who is affected by this legislation that his compensation will be set by the government, that he will be given the right to appeal but that right of appeal will be within the maximum limits set by the government. Then the government is saying that if he is not satisfied he does not have the ordinary recourse he would have in dealing with a private company of going to the courts and asking the courts to decide what is fair and equitable compensation for the loss he has suffered.
After all the years I have listened to Liberal speakers talk about the rights of the individual and tfie dangers of socialistic regimentation, they now bring down legislation telling the farmer that if he is so unfortunate as to have livestock that must be slaughtered or, in the case of Bill C-155, produce that cannot be sold, all he will be allowed is the privilege of appearing before an assessor who must hand down a figure in respect of compensation not higher than a maximum that fias been set by order in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture.
They took over when you were away.
Mr. Speaker, if this is to be the just society, then God save this country from any more of it.

Hear, hear.

If we do not have a serious epidemic of livestock disease in this country not many people may be affected. But I want to remind hon. members that we are being asked today to set a very dangerous precedent, the precedent of putting on the statute books a provision which prohibits a Canadian citizen from the right to go to the courts. We are here saying that the maximum figure recommended by the minister and approved by his colleagues is the final arbitration even though the figure they may have set may have become completely obsolete and irrelevant in view of changing conditions. This is a dangerous step.
I suggest that this is dangerous and vicious legislation and that the government ought to reconsider it before it asks us to approve this measure. I once heard Aneurin Bevan say that democracy in Germany died by the headman's axe but that in Britain it was in danger of dying from anaemia. I am not speaking of Britain but I say that in this country, if we continue to allow provisions like this to be placed on the statute books, democracy can die inch by inch by taking away from the ordinary citizen his basic rights to the point where this country will be ruled by ministerial decree and bureaucratic regulations. If this is the government's idea of a just society, then the sooner the Canadian people become aware of it and speak out, the better. I appeal to the minister to either postpone this legislation or introduce an amendment removing the provision which denies a person affected the right to go to the courts. That is the very least that should be allowed. I would like to see them granted the right to go to court and I would go a little bit farther.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
From the minister's own point of view I think he would be better off in the final analysis to permit a farmer who is disgruntled and dissatisfied to have his case heard in open court rather than being settled by an assessor appointed by the minister and restricted to the maximum figures the minister in his wisdom or the lack thereof has set for the assessor. I hope the minister will seriously reconsider this matter. I hope he will not ask the house to pass the kind of provision to be found in this legislation. If he does and other ministers follow this practice, we will be weakening the whole basis of democratic government in this country.

Mr. Speaker, a number of members of the opposition, includ-

Animal Contagious Diseases Act ing the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh), my colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave), my leader, and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) have addressed themselves to the legislation before us with specific reference to clause 2. The minister has had an opportunity on previous bills to make some kind of a response to the criticisms and appeals made by hon. members, all of whom have pointed to the serious dangers that lurk behind the provisions contained in this bill. I feel as strongly as other members about this matter but because they have pointed out the dangers clearly I see little point in repeating them at this stage.
It is my hope the minister will come from behind the curtains, get on his feet and explain why the government does not see fit to amend this legislation so we will not be in the position of legislating, as my leader and the hon. member for Swift-Current-Maple Creek put it, to prohibit citizens from having access to the courts, particularly since this matter involves property rights. My leader may have been a little facetious when he said the Liberal party seems to have become very much preoccupied with giving departments and other government bodies more and more authority, but in this case there seems to be a great deal of truth in that statement.
Over the years the Liberal party has created the impression of emphasizing the rights of individuals; yet it appears to be nonchalant about a clause such as the one contained in this bill. This is indeed surprising. It is even more surprising because of the fact that the bill is sponsored by a minister who is apparently the heir apparent to the late William Aberhart. The Liberal party has put great emphasis on the rights of individuals relative to the state. In view of this attitude there certainly is cause for complaint.
At this time I do not intend or want to make what essentially would be the same protests made by other hon. members, but I hope the minister will indicate why it is not possible to remove this provision so there will be no impingement or prohibition in respect of the right of a citizen to take a dispute to the courts. Is it so essential to the administration that we include in this bill a clause such as that contained in Bill C-156? We strongly object to the fact that a decision of an assessor will not be appealable to the courts.
There is another matter I have not heard mentioned. There is provision here that anyone who wishes to appeal the decision of an

Animal Contagious Diseases Act assessor to an appeal board must do so within three months. This strikes me as an unnecessary restriction. We realize there is some need for a restrictive clause, but in most instances of which I am aware statutes of limitation involve periods of six months or a year, and in some cases five years or more. The minister is asking for too much when he recommends to hon. members a clause which states that every appeal to an assessor shall be brought within three months of the date the owner receives notification of the decision. Why can this not be six months or a year?
The minister knows full well that during busy times of the year an individual may not find himself in a position to take some kind of formal legal action within a period of 90 days. It might be inconvenient to the government to have a longer period but the important thing is that justice should be done, and every citizen should have an ample opportunity to exercise his rights under the law. I think it is a little bit too restrictive to suggest that if an individual wants to appeal he must do so within 90 days. Let us also hear from the minister as to why it is difficult for him to envisage a longer period of time.

Mr. Speaker, according to the minister the intention of this bill is to allow the government to pay greater compensation to those who have suffered a loss. I compliment the minister on this aspect of the amendment. He would have been better off had he put a percentage or some other kind of formula in the bill in respect of the value of animals, whether it be three years or five years from now. There should be some relation between the value and the market price in arriving at a reasonable figure for compensation. Under this bill t.he minister will be the judge, the jury, the lord high executioner and the paymaster. There undoubtedly will be some conflict as a result of the minister being all of these things.
I know a farmer in my area who raises purebred bulls. Whenever I go there to buy a bull he always wants a higher price than I am willing to pay. This man, if the bull or other animal were condemned, would probably want to appeal the decision of the Department of Agriculture, whatever it might be. While I might disagree with his judgment as to the value of the animal, I think he should have the right to appeal. I think it is a good thing to have the right of appeal within the department; but ultimately, if a farmer is not
[Mr. Schreyer.l
satisfied he should have the right of appeal to a court of law. I do not suppose many farmers would go to the Exchequer Court, for example, but as long as the right is there I believe the government would tend to be more circumspect with regard to the value placed upon carcasses which are disposed of. In this respect, 1 do not intend to imply there is anything wrong with the Minister of Agriculture, because I have a good deal of respect for him despite the fact he is a Liberal.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
He isn't really.

That is right. I think the rights of people would be better protected if these things were put into writing so they knew exactly where they stood. Then, neither the government nor the farmer would be able to take unfair advantage of the act. The farmer would know he could appeal to an impartial tribunal, a judge, and he could ultimately take the matter to court and obtain a reasonable settlement if he could not do so in any other way. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will reconsider this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of things I could say in defence of this bill if I were to try and reply to all the arguments and allegations that have been made by hon. members today. However, I want to be as charitable as I can, and in keeping with that spirit I would say that we have heard a great deal of argument about many things that are not in the bill. There are three clauses to the bill. The first clause deals with removing the statutory limit on the maximum amount that can be paid for animals that are slaughtered because they have contracted named diseases. The second clause gives the right to appeal the amount which the minister may decide is proper for compensation. That is all it does. The clause does not provide for anything but
February 21, 1969

an appeal in this respect. It is rather strange to hear my hon. friends argue how unjust this provision is, because at the present time and all through the years my hon. friends opposite were in office there was no right of appeal.
How about the courts? There was always a right of appeal to them.

There was no right to appeal the amount of compensation to an assessor, a court or anyone else. My hon. friends know that. The third clause is concerned with the date of the coming into force of the measure. The reason the date is September 26 is that, in the event there are animals which show positive reaction to the named diseases, particularly tuberculosis and brucellosis, they will be disposed of without waiting and increasing the hazard involved in having the disease around the herd pending an increase in the amount paid by way of compensation. That is all there is in the bill. I think it is a useless debate to read into the bill a whole lot of other things that simply are not there.
Read clause 14A (3).

With regard to the right of appeal on the amount of compensation, that primarily involves an appeal to an assessor. That is why this person is called an assessor. In Bill C-155, the Pesticide Residue Compensation Act, we specifically and very carefully wrote in the provision that these assessors must be either judges of the Exchequer Court of Canada or judges of the superior courts of the provinces. This provision is there. It is very clear that the assessors will not be people other than those. The argument has been raised as to whether a person should have a right of appeal with regard to whether he is guilty or not guilty. That is not a question that arises at all. The only question is the amount of compensation that can be paid out of the public treasury. If that amount has been set by the minister somewhere lower than the maximum, then the farmer can appeal to the assessor to bring it up to the maximum or to a point higher. That is all that is involved.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister a question?
Yes.

Was that a slip of the tongue? The

Animal Contagious Diseases Act minister said, "Up to the maximum or something higher than the maximum."
No, something higher than had been designated by the minister.
I take it that the assessor cannot set any figure higher than the maximum which the minister has already recommended to his colleagues and which was put into an order in council?

That is right. It is very nice to see the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) back in the house and participating in the debate. He usually makes a very eloquent argument, but usually for the wrong reasons and with the wrong conclusion.
Oh, oh.

That of course happened again today, because the hon. member tried to build his argument on the basis of something that had happened respecting foot and mouth disease in Saskatchewan in February of 1952. If he had taken the trouble to inform himself, or if his colleagues had done so-and I think they should have-concerning the amended part of section 12 of the Animal Congagious Diseases Act, he would have found that this part of the act applies to four named diseases only, and one of them is not foot and mouth disease. The diseases named in the act are glanders, dourine, brucellosis and tuberculosis. That is all. There is a completely different basis for determining the amount of compensation paid in respect of diseases like foot and mouth disease because you have to introduce a program for the complete eradication of all the animals exposed to the disease. That is not applicable to this part of the act.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister another question? I understand that this provision applies only to the diseases the minister has named. But am I not correct that the appeal procedure as set out in part II of the Pesticide Residue Compensation Act, Bill C-155, will apply to all appeals under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act? If not, what will be the basis upon which payment will be made for any disease other than those outlined here, such as foot and mouth disease or hog cholera?

This is the fallacy of my hon. friend's argument and proves the point I was
5820
February 21, 1969

Animal Contagious Diseases Act making a few minutes ago, about hon. members dredging up everything they can think of with respect to this matter and trying to apply it to the three clauses of the bill. I could go into a great deal of detailed explanation as to how values are arrived at for other diseases. But to put it very briefly, under an eradication program market values are used. In some cases the carcass has no salvage value because it is destroyed completely. This is not the case, for example, with animals which do not have an active disease but in fact show a positive reaction to a test for brucellosis or tuberculosis after proper inspection by our inspectors at the slaughtering plants. The salvage value of those carcasses is as high as if they did not show a positive reaction at all. Over and above that is the compensation which we are setting out in this measure.
Therefore, the brief answer is that with regard to those animals which have no salvage value at all, the market value is set down by a formula that we have used, very satisfactorily I may say, for a long period of time. In this way, we have arrived at the value and compensation that should be paid.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the minister quite understood my question. With respect to these other diseases like foot and mouth disease or hog cholera, is there no right of appeal, or is the procedure for appeal as set out in this legislation to be applicable in the case of other diseases? Or is there no right of appeal with respect to them?

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure about the right of appeal in those cases, but there is a completely different procedure. For example, a committee is set up consisting of somebody representing the department, the nominee of the person or persons involved, and someone neutral. This committee decides on the value of animals in the case where an eradication program is required because of contraction of a contagious disease.
Why not in the case of these other diseases?

In many cases that is the procedure if a large number of animals is involved. However, what my hon. friend does not seem to realise is that there is a continuing program of testing throughout the country of

what appear to be healthy animals. Whenever we find any animals that show a positive reaction to the test they are taken out of the herd, and compensation is paid to the producer on the basis outlined. Up until this time, there has been no appeal from a decision of the minister or the department.
The question was asked why we put the phrase "with such modifications as circumstances require" in clause 2(3). As far as I understand it, this is the English translation of the latin phrase that is used, "mutatis mutandis". These words do not change the provisions of the compensation act but allow for differences in wording between the two acts. Thus, they are a link between the two acts. However, some differences have to be taken into account so far as administration is concerned.
A number of questions were asked about whether or not the amount of compensation would be high enough, and whether crossbreds and so on, should be included. As I said in the committee-I think it is well to repeat myself here-the maximum amount that can be paid by way of compensation over and above the salvage value of the carcass today is $70 for a grade animal and $140 for a purebred animal. A purebred is defined as an animal that has been registered or that is eligible to be registered, whether registered or not.
I am going to recommend to the Governor in Council that these values be changed to $120 for grade animals and $200 for purebred animals. This is a very substantial increase; in percentage terms it is in the neighbourhood of 70 per cent. The fact of the matter is that these statutory limits have not been changed for 11 years, since 1958. Therefore, we think there is some justification for changing them.
Notwithstanding that the amounts may be higher, because of the very successful program we have been carrying on for a number of years to eradicate these diseases, the total amount charged to the federal treasury will, in our view, be substantially less under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. Statistics bear out that the program has been very successful over a long period of time.

I do not want to interrupt the minister's train of thought, but before he leaves that point I should like to ask him how it is possible to set a maximum figure when dealing with purebred livestock. At every fair one sees purebred livestock selling at very
February 21, 1969	COMMONS
fancy figures. Therefore, I would think that purebred livestock varies in value greatly, and I should like to know how it is possible to set a maximum figure. Is the assessor not to be allowed complete freedom, instead of some maximum being imposed? For example, the animal in question might be a prize bull that would fetch thousands of dollars; in such a case a maximum of $200 seems absurd.

This act is not intended to compensate at the kind of values that are sometimes put upon animals at auction sales. If anybody has a very valuable animal, such as the one described by the hon. member, it is usually insured. Certainly, insurance is available for such animals. That is one reason.
Another reason is that in some cases it is possible, through a reasonably satisfactory process, to arrive at a value for such animals. We take the position that there are so many exceptions to the rule in the process of arriving at the value of some of these animals that we need to set down a maximum so that everybody is treated equally and fairly.
I should also point out to the hon. member that the cost to the federal treasury is not simply the cost of the compensation paid to the farmer. A great deal of additional cost is involved in helping the farmer rid his farm of these diseases and to clean up his herd. This is of equal, indeed far greater, value to the farmer as the actual dollars paid to him in compensation. If we used market values or adopted some other means of doing away with the maximum amount of compensation, we would, it seems to me, be opening the door to a lot of litigation and expressions of opinion as to the value of animals. I do not mind this if those values are properly tested in the market place. But, of course, they cannot be tested. There is no way positively to test market value of an animal once it has become sick or has contracted one of these diseases. Therefore, we need to establish a maximum.
I might say to the hon. member that the point he makes has not proved to be a great problem so far as high priced animals are concerned because, in the first place, they are eligible for insurance and in most cases are insured. I do not think anybody could say that there is no way for producers to defend themselves in this kind of situation, which would be the case for lower priced or grade animals.

Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to ask the minister a question. I am

Animal Contagious Diseases Act not sure that the assumption he has made is correct and I should like to ask for clarification. The minister chastised a previous speaker for dealing with hog cholera and foot and mouth disease. The minister indicated that these diseases were not relevant to subclauses (1), (2) and (3) of clause 2. Is it not a fact that the section of the act that we are amending, section 14, which is the appeal provision, is not restricted simply to brucellosis and t.b., but applies to the act in its entirety?

I will have an answer to that question in a moment. I think that when I made that statement I was talking about clause 1, which is the clause that removes the statutory maximum that is set down for the four diseases I named a few moments ago. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) had a lot to say about this question, but what he apparently does not understand is that we are not taking away anybody's rights. We are in fact granting a right of appeal which has never existed before. I find it hard to understand any of these arguments seeking to show we are taking something away when really we are extending the right of persons to appeal on a matter which involves a charge to the public treasury. Appellants would be questioning the minister's decision as to how much would be the proper compensation. In most cases it will only be the amount which will be the subject of an appeal, though there is a possibility of appeal in cases where no payment is to be made, and where a more favourable ruling is sought. But in most cases the question of substance will be the opinion of the assessor as to whether or not, within the minima and maxima laid down in the regulations, the amount was fair.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I cannot understand how the hon. member can argue from both sides of the fence at the same time. At one point he told us that judges of the Exchequer Court and of the Superior Courts of the provinces should not be involved at all.

assessors.

Extrajudicial.

All right; whatever the word was. Immediately after saying that, he told us these cases should be appealable to the courts, where the very same men would be seated.

assessors.

I believe I have answered all the questions hon. members have asked me. There were one or two further questions, though. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) asked whether an assessor could award more than the maximum. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) asked that question too.
We are now taking out of the legislation the statutory limits of $70 and $140 respectively and we are providing that these amounts shall be determined by order in council. In other words, parliament is saying in this session, and has been saying in 1958 and on all those other occasions when this act has been before it, that there should be a certain maxima. speechtext:
Bill C-157 is another in a series of bills respecting regulations with regard to the agriculture industry. This particular bill also deals with an allied industry, the chemical industry in connection with pesticides manufactured by it and applied to products grown in Canada. This measure provides an even greater indication of the arbitrary powers being taken by this government.
I was happy to hear the minister, in his short address, explain the workings of the Standing Committee on Agriculture. He said we had time to study this bill clause by clause. Although the theory of such a standing committee may be good, the operation of it leaves much to be desired.
There are two large industries, the chemical industry and the agriculture industry, influenced by the regulations in this legislation. This bill intrudes on the normal operation of these industries. When the committee was about to study this bill clause by clause, I was shocked to learn the government did not intend to call witnesses from these industries to present their opinions as to whether or not,
DEBATES	5825
Animal Contagious Diseases Act the bill was advantageous and to express opinions on the various clauses of this bill. Although both these industries were to be regulated and regimented, neither were going to be given the opportunity to make representations. It was only after a great deal of discussion that the chemical industry was permitted to make representations.
The evidence provided by the representatives of the chemical industry was very informative and formed the basis for one minor amendment to the bill. It was an historic feat to have even one amendment accepted in committee which was not produced by the government. The provisions of this bill deal with most facets of the chemicals involved, that is, the composition, registration, packaging, storage, transportation, sale, utilization and a strict examination of their effects. We must be very careful when intruding to this extent on the companies involved. We must not be too cumbersome in granting adequate protection to the users of the products involved. We must not make it impossible for these two industries to take advantage of the newest developments.
This bill gives more rights to an inspector of the government than are given to an officer of the R.C.M.P. The fact that an inspector is a government employee and shows his identification, gives him the right to go into any building or property and require every person to assist him in his inspection. He is given the right to demand all books and papers he may deem necessary. In essence, an inspector is given all the powers of an officer of the law. He can take upon himself the power of controlling the distribution of such chemicals. As a matter of fact, he can require companies to cease the manufacture of a chemical. He can stop the transportation of it, or the utilization of it. He can impound all quantities wherever they are found on his assertion that they do not meet the requirements of this bill in respect of labelling, storage, transportation, or usage, or on the ground that the chemical may cause some danger either directly or residually to the food utilized for human consumption.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Absolute power is granted to an individual to intrude in the normal operations of two industries. Inspectors will operate under the regulations made under this bill, but those regulations are not spelled out. They are merely stated to be such regulations as may be prescribed., I object to these agricultural bills which do not make provision for an
February 21, 1969

Animal Contagious Diseases Act appeal to a court after an assessor has made a determination. It is left arbitrarily in the hands of a single inspector to stop the normal business of two industries.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it is even worse than that. A company may spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on the preparation of a chemical specifically designed to aid agriculture. Under this legislation, the Company must apply to the government for registration before it can dispose, sell, transport or package the chemical for commercial use. In the standing committee, we heard evidence that sometimes it takes months before a determination is made by the department as to whether or not registration should be granted. With respect to the registration of a new chemical, it is quite possible that it will take weeks or months to obtain the necessary information from the various laboratories and testing fields. We have discovered that registration may be held up because of a difference of opinion between two government departments, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Agriculture.
This bill is another example of government intrusion into business under the guise of benefiting the public. The intent is good, and we in the Official Opposition in no way say that the welfare of the people of Canada should not be protected to the nlh degree. This is necessary but when arbitrary powers are given to individuals, surely equal powers of review are necessary.
Ini the standing committee we heard from officials of the department that the registration of chemicals could take a matter of days, and that speed was essential when dealing with chemicals that are used on a seasonal basis. But when representatives of the industry appeared before the committee they said it sometimes was not a matter of days but of months, and in fact on occasion a matter of years before a decision could be reached. People engaged in agriculture cannot wait for years. In many instances they cannot wait for months. Farmers must have chemicals to deal with specific problems as they arise or else suffer crop failures.
I feel that when a product has been refused registration, the company concerned should have the right of direct and fast appeal. It should have the right of direct appeal to a minister or to the department when it feels there has been undue delay in granting registration. A company should have a right to

appeal when there has been seizure or detention of a product on the decision of a single inspector. It should have a right to appeal against a decision respecting packaging, labelling and advertising when such decision has stopped the normal distribution of the product. A company should have a right to appeal when the government contends that an indictable offence has been committed by one of its agents or employees.
When representatives of the industry appeared before the standing committee the government relented and introduced an amendment to the bill granting the right of appeal. But then, as the government does in so many cases, it added the rider "subject to such regulations as may be prescribed." In my considered view, this killed the request made on behalf of the industry. I am concerned about this legislation brought before us under the guise of being of direct benefit to agriculture because it has become so cumbered with regulations, and so one-sided against industry. I feel the good intentions which gave rise to it have been nullified. I have great hesitation in supporting the bill, although I do believe that the primary intent was good.
