This saving is made by the Canadian people. The expenditure of money in this society does not take place as a result of the beneficence of any particular trust company either. This money is going to be spent in one way or another, just as it will be saved in one way or another. What is important is how it is going to be spent, and that is the real point of this debate.
Is this money to be collected by a trust company which puts its money into areas where it will make the most profit without regard for social consequence? Is it to be collected by a public agency, which is the way we would like to see it done, which would be concerned about the almost three quarters of all Canadians who cannot afford their own homes? Mr, Speaker, an observation of that sort, however kind and generous to me, casts some doubt upon my opinion of Your Honour. Methinks you are mistaken. The bill relating to the Huron and Erie Mortgage Corporation is the matter before the house. There are one or two things I wish to say in connection with this corporation. Although they have been said before, I think it is necessary to reiterate them because they deal with the substance of the bill and the substance of a great deal of misunderstanding that arose in the committee as well as in the minds of many who have read the evidence upon which the report of the committee was founded.
The Huron and Erie Mortgage Corporation has at the moment an authorized capital of $10 million divided into five million shares of $2 each. It seeks, in effect, to double the share capital and the number of shares, but retain the par value of the shares and be in a position to raise, by reason of the additional sale of its share capital presumably, another $10 million. As I understand the situation, nearly all the authorized shares of the company have now been distributed and are outstanding.
There is, as was pointed out in the committee, a relationship between the amount of money a mortgage company can lend and the

amount of money that it has in the treasury, or the amount of its share capital, plus the surplus. I did not find out, and I doubt very much whether this matter was gone into in the committee, what the surplus position of the company might be. There is no reference to it that I can find. I have looked at the trust and loan companies financial survey of industrials. This survey covers the Huron and Erie Mortgage Corporation and lists the consolidated balance sheet, but only the main items. It is difficult for me to pull out from that what the surplus of a company might be. It could be listed under another name, or it may be divided and put into other accounts or other sorts of funds., Therefore, I do not know what the surplus figure is. In any event, there is a ratio of 15 to 1 in terms of the lending of money, related to the amount of share capital plus the surplus. I assume this means, speaking in very small numbers and only by way of illustration, that for every $100 the company has as a result of the sale of shares, it will be able to lend $1,500 for mortgages, as a maximum.

That is the theory behind the operation of this kind of corporation, namely, to keep your money in circulation. If it is more correct to say, in the jargon of the legal and accounting professions, that it can borrow 15 times more than is borrowed from it, I am content to put it that way. However, what I was getting at is that the ratio of 15 to 1 is permitted by order in council. There is a statutory amount beyond which the corporation cannot go after receiving permission

At this point, I should like to read from the evidence given by Mr. Humphrys, the Superintendent of Insurance, to the committee on January 21. His evidence was on this very point, and I should like to put his words on the record because they may help to clarify my argument.
Mr. Humphrys, in reply to a question, said:
The multiple for trust companies is 12J times the capital and surplus, but it may be increased to 15 times subject to approval by the Treasury Board. For mortgage loan companies the limit stated in the law is four times, but this may be also increased 15 times subject to application by the company and approval by the Treasury Board. Both of these companies-
He was referring to Canada Trust and Huron and Erie Mortgage Corporation.
-had their ratio approved at 15 times which is the maximum permissible under the law.
I understand that a proposition is being put forward and is being looked upon very favourably by the government that this 15 to 1 ratio be increased to 20 to 1. If this is the case, the company will automatically be in a better position so far as its borrowings and subsequent lendings are concerned. But even on the basis of a ratio of 15 to 1, the corporation, with the expectation of raising an additional $10 million through the sale of shares, will be able to increase its potential borrowing position and, consequently, its potential lending position by an additional $150 million.
If this is the sort of money the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton was talking about being pumped into the mortgage lending field, it is very interesting and gratifying to note that it is the case. If the ratio is increased to 20 to 1, which I am told is quite possible, the amount would be increased even more and there would be a couple of hundred million dollars at least in additional money available for the company to borrow and, subsequently, to lend. The $150 million extra' that one can assume, on the basis of the surface presentation of the company, would be available for mortgages will not be available at all. On one occasion I was in Vancouver and visited the offices of three or four trust, mortgage and loan companies. I spoke to various officers of those companies. I do not know whether the Huron and Erie was one of the companies because I cannot remember the names, but they were all large, well established companies known across Canada.
I asked the officials of all of these companies what were the prospects of money being made available in communities such as Terrace, Prince Rupert and Smithers, these smaller, out of the way communities far removed from metropolitan areas of the nation. The officials of these companies gave me, in different terms and tones, the same answer. In effect, they said: "We can't be bothered because we are doing quite well in the city of Vancouver. They prefer to concentrate their money in the cities where all they need do is cross the street or make a phone call to reinvest it.
The fact that Huron and Erie Mortgage Corporation has over the years, not just this week or last month, not bothered to exert itself by providing mortgage money in rural areas concerns me. When I hear the figure of 88 per cent I am reminded of the report

The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) asked Mr. Taylor, who appeared before the committee, questions about the priorities of spending in the public and private sectors of our economy.
